name: Marcus Argentarius
bio: Marcus Argentarius was an epigrammatist of the Garland of Philippus, writing around the turn of the era. He is best known for sharply observed love and banquet epigrams.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him by name.

poems.title: Book V, 16
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Golden-horned Moon, and all ye stars that shine around and sink into the bosom of Ocean, look on this! Perfumed Ariste is gone and hath left me alone, and for six days I “seek the witch in vain. But we shall catch her notwithstanding, if I put the silver hounds of Cypris on her track.

poems.title: Book V, 32
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: You do everything, Melissa, that your namesake the flower-loving bee does. I know this and take it to heart. You drop honey from your lips, when you sweetly kiss, and when you ask for money you sting me most unkindly.

poems.title: Book V, 63
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Antigone, I used to think you were Sicilian, but now you have become an Aetolian® I have become a Mede.

poems.title: Book V, 89
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: That is not love if one, trusting his judicious eyes, wishes to possess a beauty. But he who seeing a homely face is pierced by the arrows and loves, set alight by fury of the heart—that is love, that is fire ; for beauty delights equally all who are good judges of form.

poems.title: Book V, 102
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: “You will see Dioclea, a rather slim little Venus, but blessed with a sweet disposition.” “Then there won't be much between us, but falling on her thin bosom I will lie all the nearer to her heart.”

poems.title: Book V, 104
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Take off these nets, Lysidice, you tease, and don’t roll your hips on purpose, as you walk. The folds of your thin dress cling well to you, and all your charms are visible as if "naked, and yet are invisible. If this seems amusing to you, I myself will dress in gauze too (hoc erectum bysso velabo.)

poems.title: Book V, 110
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Pour in ten ladles of Lysidice, cup-bearer, and of charming Euphrante give me one ladle. You will say I love Lysidice best. No! I swear by sweet Bacchus, whom I drain from this cup. But Euphrante is as one to ten. Doth not the light of the moon that is single overcome that of countless stars ?

poems.title: Book V, 113
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: You fell in love, Sosicrates, when rich; now you are poor, you are in love no longer. What an admirable cure is hunger! And Menophila, who used to call you her sweety and her darling Adonis, now asks your name. “What man art thou, and whence, thy city where?”’+ You have perforce learnt the meaning of the saying, “None is the friend of him who has nothing.”

poems.title: Book V, 116
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: The love of women is best for those men who are serious in their attachments. Si vero et masculus amor tibi placet, scio remedium, quo sedabis pravum istum morbum. Invertens Menophilam pulchriclunem crede masculum Menophilum amplecti.

poems.title: Book V, 118
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Istas, though thy perfumed breath be ten times sweeter than spikenard, awake, and take this garland in thy dear hands. Now it is blooming, but as dawn approaches thou wilt see it fading, a symbol of thine own fresh youth.

poems.title: Book V, 127
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: I was very fond of a young girl called Alcippe, and once, having succeeded in persuading her, I brought her secretly to my room. Both our hearts were beating, lest any superfluous person should surprise us and witness our secret love. But her mother overheard her talk, and looking in suddenly, said, “We go shares, my daughter.”’

poems.title: Book V, 128
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Breast to breast supporting my bosom on hers, and pressing her sweet lips to mine I clasped Antigone close with naught between us. Touching the rest, of which the lamp was entered as witness, Iam silent.

poems.title: Book VI, 201
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Euphrante, when she was happily delivered of the burden of her womb, dedicated in the temple of Artemis her sandals and beautiful head-band, and this scented curl cut from her lovely locks, her zone, too, and this fine under-vest, and the bright band that encompassed her bosom.

poems.title: Book VI, 248
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Rest here, consecrated to Cypris henceforth, my tipsy flagon, sister of the sweet wine-cup, devotee of Bacchus, liquid-voiced, boon-companion in the “equal feast,’ slim-necked daughter of our dining club, self-taught minister of men, sweetest confidant of lovers, ever ready to serve at the banquet; rest here, a lordly gift from Marcus who sang thy praises, thou tippler, when he dedicated thee, the old companion of his wanderings.

poems.title: Book VI, 333: A Love Epigram misplaced
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Thrice hast thou sneezed, dear lamp! Is it, perchance, to tell me that delightful Antigone is coming to my chamber? For if, my lord, this be true, thou shalt stand by the tripod, like Apollo, and prophesy to men.

poems.title: Book VII, 364
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Myro made this tomb for her grasshopper and cicada, sprinkling a little dust over them both and weeping regretfully over their pyre; for the songster was seized by Hades and the other by Persephone.

poems.title: Book VII, 374
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: My ill-fated body was covered by the sea, and beside the waves my mother, Lysidice, wept for me much, gazing at my false and empty tomb, while my evil genius sent my lifeless corpse to be tossed with the sea-gulls on the deep. My name was Pnytagoras and I met my fate on the Aegean, when taking in the stern cables because of the north-wind. Yet not even so did I end my voyage, but from my ship I embarked on another boat among the dead.

poems.title: Book VII, 384
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Of Aristomache the talkative friend of the vine, who loved Bacchus much more than did his nurse Ino, when she went under holy earth, and the spirit of her who had enjoyed so many a cup had utterly faded, said “Shake, Minos, the light urn. I will fetch the dark water from Acheron; for I too slew a young husband.” This falsehood she told in order that even among the dead she should be able to look at a jar.

poems.title: Book VII, 395
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: This is the cenotaph of Callaeschrus, whom the deep undid as he was crossing the Libyan main, then when the force of Orion at the stormy season of his baneful setting” stirred the sea from its depths. The sea-monsters devoured his wave-tossed corpse, and the stone bears but this empty inscription.

poems.title: Book VII, 403
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Psythus, who used to take to the pleasant banquets of the young men the venal ladies that they desired, that hunter of weak girls, who earned a disgraceful wage by dealing in human flesh, lies here But cast not thou stones at his tomb, wayfarer, nor bid another do so. He is dead and buried. Spare him, not because he was content to gain his living so, but because as keeper of common women he dissuaded young men from adultery.

poems.title: Book IX, 87
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: No longer warble, blackbird, by the oak-tree, no longer perch on the highest branch and call. This tree is thy enemy; hie thee to where the vine mounts with shady green leaves. Set thy feet on its branch and sing by it, pouring shrill notes from thy throat. For the oak bears the mistletoe which is the foe of birds, but the vine bears grape-clusters ; and Bacchus loves songsters.

poems.title: Book IX, 161
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: As I was turning over the pages of a volume of Hesiod, I suddenly saw Pyrrhe approaching. Throwing the book on the ground I exclaimed: “Wh should I be bothered by your works, old Hesiod ?”

poems.title: Book IX, 221
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: I ser upon the signet-ring Love, whom none can escape, driving a chariot drawn by mighty lions. One hand menaces their necks with the whip, the other guides the reins ; about him is shed abundant bloom of grace. I shudder as I look on the destroyer of men, for he who can tame wild beasts will not show the least mercy to mortals.

poems.title: Book IX, 229
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: My ancient boon-companion, friend of the vintner’s measures, sweet babbler with the gentle laugh, pretty mouth and long neck, my flagon, ever knowing the secret of my poverty but contributing little to relieve it, I have waited for thee long, but I hold thee now. Would I had thee unmixed and unwedded, coming like a maiden undefiled to her husband.

poems.title: Book IX, 246
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Thou art broken, sweet flagon, dear to the winebibbers, and hast shed from thy belly all the liquor of Bacchus. For from afar fell on thee, with a dreadful crash, a stone like a thunderbolt hurled by the hand, not of Zeus (Dios), but of Dion. And when it smote thee there was much laughter and many gibes, and a great noise among the company. I do not lament thee, flagon, who didst give birth to Bacchus the crier of Ehoe, for thy fate has been the same as Semele’s.

poems.title: Book IX, 270
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: I keep revel, gazing at the golden dance of the stars of evening, nor do I rudely disturb the converse of others. Tossing my hair that scatters flowers, I awake with musical fingers the deep-toned lyre. And in doing so I lead an orderly life, for the order of the universe itself lacks not a Lyre and a Crown.

poems.title: Book IX, 286
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Why hast thou, chanticleer, robbed me of beloved sleep, and the sweet image of Pyrrha has flown away from my bed? Is this my recompense for bringing thee up and making thee, ill-starred fowl, the lord of all the egg-laying herd in my house? I swear by the altar and sceptre of Serapis, no more shalt thou call in the night, but shalt lie on that altar by which I have sworn.

poems.title: Book IX, 554
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Clam, Heraclea, pulchris juvenibus ore morigeraris. For long all the town says it of you. How do you venture to do such a shameful thing? Did anyone catch you by your beautiful hair and force you to it? Or is it because your pretty name is derived from Heracles that in your depravity you choose to kiss his wife Hebe (pubem juvenum).

poems.title: Book IX, 732
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Stranger, if thou seest my herdsman, give him this message, that the sculptor Myron tied me up here.

poems.title: Book X, 4
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Loose the long hawsers from your well-moored ships, and spreading your easily-hoisted sails set to sea, merchant captain. For the storms have taken flight and tenderly laughing Zephyr now makes the blue wave gentle as a girl. Already the swallow, fond parent, is building with its lisping lips its chamber out of mud and straw, and flowers spring up in the land; therefore listen to Priapus and undertake any kind of navigation.

poems.title: Book X, 18
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Guests, let Dionysus and Aphrodite, who loves dalliance, delight thee, and the sweet Muses too with their letters. Their wisdom thou hast plucked ; but enter now on her loves and drain his dear bowls.

poems.title: Book XI, 26
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: I feel drunk with wine; but who shall save me from Bacchus who makes my limbs totter? How unjust a god have I encountered, since while I carry thee, Bacchus, by thee, in return, I am carried astray.

poems.title: Book XI, 28
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Dead, five feet of earth shall be thine and thou shalt not look on the delights of life or on the rays of the sun. So take the cup of unmixed wine and drain it rejoicing, Cincius, with thy arm round thy lovely wife. But if thou deemest wisdom to be immortal, know that Cleanthes and Zeno went to deep Hades.

poems.title: Book XI, 320
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text: Philostratus loved Antigone. He was poorer by five cubits, poor fellow, than Irus. The cold, however, taught him a sweet remedy ; for tucking up his knees (with antza gonata) he slept so, stranger, with Antigone.

poems.title: Love and the Scholar (Mackail)
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Once when turning over the Book of Hesiod in my hands, suddenly I saw Pyrrha coming in; and casting the book to the ground from my hand, I cried out, Why bring your works to me, old Hesiod?

poems.title: Flown Love (Mackail)
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Golden-horned Moon, thou seest this, and you fiery-shining Stars whom Ocean takes into his breast, how perfume-breathing Ariste has gone and left me alone, and this is the sixth day I cannot find the witch. But we will seek her notwithstanding; surely I will send the silver sleuth-hounds of the Cyprian on her track.

poems.title: Inter Minora Sidera (Mackail)
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Pour ten cups for Lysidice, and for beloved Euphrante, slave, give me one cup. Thou wilt say I love Lysidice more? No, by sweet Bacchus, whom I drink deep in this bowl; Euphrante for me, one against ten; for the one splendour of the moon also outshines the innumerable stars.

poems.title: To a Blackbird Singing (Mackail)
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: No longer now warble on the oak, no longer sing, O blackbird, sitting on the topmost spray; this tree is thine enemy; hasten where the vine rises in clustering shade of silvered leaves; on her bough rest the sole of thy foot, around her sing and pour the shrill music of thy mouth; for the oak carries mistletoe baleful to birds, and she the grape-cluster; and the Wine-god cherishes singers.

poems.title: The Flower of Youth (Mackail)
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Sweet-breathed Isias, though thy sleep be tenfold spice, awake and take this garland in thy dear hands, which, blooming now, thou wilt see withering at daybreak, the likeness of a maiden's prime.

poems.title: Light Love (Mackail)
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Thou wert loved when rich, Sosicrates, but being poor thou art loved no longer; what magic has hunger! And she who before called thee spice and darling Adonis, Menophila, now inquires thy name. Who and whence of men art thou? where is thy city? Surely thou art dull in learning this saying, that none is friend to him who has nothing.

poems.title: Angelorum Chori (Mackail)
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I hold revel, regarding the golden choir of the stars at evening, nor do I spurn the dances of others; but garlanding my hair with flowers that drop their petals over me, I waken the melodious harp into passion with musical hands; and doing thus I lead a well-ordered life, for the order of the heavens too has its Lyre and Crown.

poems.title: One Event (Mackail)
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Five feet shalt thou possess as thou liest dead, nor shalt see the pleasant things of life nor the beams of the sun; then joyfully lift and drain the unmixed cup of wine, O Cincius, holding a lovely wife in thine arms; and if philosophy say that thy mind is immortal, know that Cleanthes and Zeno went down to deep Hades.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.16: μήνη χρυσόκερως, δέρκευ τάδε, καὶ
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
μήνη χρυσόκερως, δέρκευ τάδε, καὶ περιλαμπεῖς
ἀστέρες, οὓς κόλποις Ὠκεανὸς δέχεται,
ὥς με μόνον προλιποῦσα μυρόπνοος ᾤχετʼ Ἀρίστη·
ἑκταίην δʼ εὑρεῖν τὴν μάγον οὐ δύναμαι.
ἀλλʼ ἔμπης αὐτὴν ζωγρήσομεν, ἢν ἐπιπέμψω
Κύπριδος ἰχνευτὰς ἀργυρέους σκύλακας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.32: ποιεῖς πάντα, Μέλισσα, φιλανθέος ἔργα
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
ποιεῖς πάντα, Μέλισσα, φιλανθέος ἔργα μελίσσης·
οἶδα καὶ ἐς κραδίην τοῦτο, γύναι, τίθεμαι.
καὶ μέλι μὲν στάζεις ὑπὸ χείλεσιν ἡδὺ φιλεῦσα·
ἢν δʼ αἰτῇς, κέντρῳ τύμμα φέρεις ἄδικον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.63: Ἀντιγόνη, Σικελὴ πάρος ἦσθά μοι·
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
Ἀντιγόνη, Σικελὴ πάρος ἦσθά μοι· ὡς δʼ ἐγενήθης
Αἰτωλή, κἀγὼ Μῆδος ἰδοὺ γέγονα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.89: οὐκ ἔσθʼ οὗτος ἔρως, εἴ
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
οὐκ ἔσθʼ οὗτος ἔρως, εἴ τις καλὸν εἶδος ἔχουσαν
βούλετʼ ἔχειν, φρονίμοις ὄμμασι πειθόμενος·
ἀλλʼ ὅστις κακόμορφον ἰδών, τετορημένος ἰοῖς
στέργει, μαινομένης ἐκ φρενὸς αἰθόμενος,
οὗτος ἔρως, πῦρ τοῦτο· τὰ γὰρ καλὰ πάντας ὁμοίως
τέρπει τοὺς κρίνειν εἶδος ἐπισταμένους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.102: τὴν ἰσχνὴν Διόκλειαν, ἀσαρκοτέρην Ἀφροδίτην,
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
τὴν ἰσχνὴν Διόκλειαν, ἀσαρκοτέρην Ἀφροδίτην,
ὄψεαι, ἀλλὰ καλοῖς ἤθεσι τερπομένην.
οὐ πολύ μοι τὸ μεταξὺ γενήσεται· ἀλλʼ ἐπὶ λεπτὰ
στέρνα πεσὼν, ψυχῆς κείσομαι ἐγγυτάτω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.104: αἶρε τὰ δίκτυα ταῦτα, κακόσχολε,
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
αἶρε τὰ δίκτυα ταῦτα, κακόσχολε, μηδʼ ἐπίτηδες
ἰσχίον ἐρχομένη σύστρεφε, Λυσιδίκη.
εὖ σε περισφίγγει λεπτὸς στολιδώμασι πέπλος,
πάντα δέ σου βλέπεται γυμνά, καὶ οὐ βλέπεται.
εἰ τόδε σοι χαρίεν καταφαίνεται, αὐτὸς ὁμοίως
ὀρθὸν ἔχων βύσσῳ τοῦτο περισκεπάσω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.110: ἔγχει Λυσιδίκης κυάθους δέκα, τῆς
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
ἔγχει Λυσιδίκης κυάθους δέκα, τῆς δὲ ποθεινῆς
Εὐφράντης ἕνα μοι, λάτρι, δίδου κύαθον.
φήσεις Λυσιδίκην με φιλεῖν πλέον. οὐ μὰ τὸν ἡδὺν
Βάκχον, ὃν ἐν ταύτῃ λαβροποτῶ κύλικι·
ἀλλά μοι Εὐφράντη μία πρὸς δέκα· καὶ γὰρ ἀπείρους
ἀστέρας ἓν μήνης φέγγος ὑπερτίθεται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.113: ἠράσθης πλουτῶν, Σωσίκρατες· ἀλλὰ πένης
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
ἠράσθης πλουτῶν, Σωσίκρατες· ἀλλὰ πένης ὢν
οὐκέτʼ ἐρᾷς· λιμὸς φάρμακον οἷον ἔχει.
ἡ δὲ πάρος σε καλεῦσα μύρον καὶ τερπνὸν Ἄδωνιν
Μηνοφίλα, νῦν σου τοὔνομα πυνθάνεται,
τίς πόθεν εἶς ἀνδρῶν, πόθι τοι πτόλις; ἦ μόλις ἔγνως
τοῦτʼ ἔπος, ὡς οὐδεὶς οὐδὲν ἔχοντι φίλος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.116: θῆλυς ἔρως κάλλιστος ἐνὶ θνητοῖσι
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
θῆλυς ἔρως κάλλιστος ἐνὶ θνητοῖσι τέτυκται,
ὅσσοις ἐς φιλίην σεμνὸς ἔνεστι νόος.
εἰ δὲ καὶ ἀρσενικὸν στέργεις πόθον, οἶδα διδάξαι
φάρμακον, ᾧ παύσεις τὴν δυσέρωτα νόσον.
στρέψας Μηνοφίλαν εὐίσχιον, ἐν φρεσὶν ἔλπου
αὐτὸν ἔχειν κόλποις ἄρσενα Μηνόφιλον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.118: Ἰσιὰς ἡδύπνευστε, καὶ εἰ δεκάκις
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
Ἰσιὰς ἡδύπνευστε, καὶ εἰ δεκάκις μύρον ὄσδεις,
ἔγρεο καὶ δέξαι χερσὶ φίλαις στέφανον,
ὃν νῦν μὲν θάλλοντα, μαραινόμενον δὲ πρὸς ἠῶ
ὄψεαι, ὑμετέρης σύμβολον ἡλικίης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.127: παρθένον Ἀλκίππην ἐφίλουν μέγα, καί
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
παρθένον Ἀλκίππην ἐφίλουν μέγα, καί ποτε πείσας
αὐτὴν λαθριδίως εἶχον ἐπὶ κλισίῃ.
ἀμφοτέρων δὲ στέρνον ἐπάλλετο, μή τις ἐπέλθῃ,
μή τις ἴδῃ τὰ πόθων κρυπτὰ περισσοτέρων.
μητέρα δʼ οὐκ ἔλαθεν κείνης λάλον ἀλλʼ ἐσιδοῦσα
ἐξαπίνης, Ἑρμῆς κοινός, ἔφη. θύγατερ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.128: στέρνα περὶ στέρνοις, μαστῷ δʼ
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
στέρνα περὶ στέρνοις, μαστῷ δʼ ἔπι μαστὸν ἐρείσας,
χείλεά τε γλυκεροῖς χείλεσι συμπιέσας
Ἀντιγόνης, καὶ χρῶτα λαβὼν πρὸς χρῶτα, τὰ λοιπὰ
σιγῶ, μάρτυς ἐφʼ οἷς λύχνος ἐπεγράφετο.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.201: σάνδαλα καὶ μίτρην περικαλλέα, τόν
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
σάνδαλα καὶ μίτρην περικαλλέα, τόν τε μυρόπνουν
βόστρυχον ὡραίων οὖλον ἀπὸ πλοκάμων,
καὶ ζώνην, καὶ λεπτὸν ὑπένδυμα τοῦτο Χιτῶνος,
καὶ τὰ περὶ στέρνοις ἀγλαὰ μαστόδετα,
ἔμβρυον εὐώδινος ἐπεὶ φύγε νηδύος ὄγκον,
Εὐφράντη νηῷ θῆκεν ὕπʼ Ἀρτέμιδος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.248: Κύπριδι κεῖσο, λάγυνε μεθυσφαλές, αὐτίκα
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
Κύπριδι κεῖσο, λάγυνε μεθυσφαλές, αὐτίκα δῶρον
κεῖσο, κασιγνήτη νεκταρέης κύλικος,
βακχιάς, ὑγρόφθογγε, συνέστιε δαιτὸς ἐίσης,
στειναύχην ψήφου συμβολικῆς θύγατερ,
θνητοῖς αὐτοδίδακτε διήκονε, μύστι φιλούντων
ἡδίστη, δείπνων ὅπλον ἑτοιμότατον
εἴης ἐκ Μάρκου γέρας ἀγλαόν, ὃς σέ, φίλοινε,
ᾔνεσεν, ἀρχαίην σύμπλανον ἀνθέμενος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.333: ἤδη, φίλτατε λύχνε, τρὶς ἔπταρες·
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
ἤδη, φίλτατε λύχνε, τρὶς ἔπταρες· ἦ τάχα τερπνὴν
εἰς θαλάμους ἥξειν Ἀντιγόνην προλέγεις;
εἰ γάρ, ἄναξ, εἴη τόδʼ ἐτήτυμον, οἷος Ἀπόλλων
θνητοῖς μάντις ἔσῃ καὶ σὺ παρὰ τρίποδι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.364: Ἀκρίδι καὶ τέττιγι Μυρὼ τόδε
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
Ἀκρίδι καὶ τέττιγι Μυρὼ τόδε θήκατο σῆμα,
λιτὴν ἀμφοτέροις χερσὶ βαλοῦσα κόνιν,
ἵμερα δακρύσασα πυρῆς ἔπι· τὸν γὰρ ἀοιδὸν
ᾅδης, τὴν δʼ ἑτέρην ἥρπασε Περσεφόνη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.374: δύσμορος ἐκρύφθην πόντῳ νέκυς, ὃν
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
δύσμορος ἐκρύφθην πόντῳ νέκυς, ὃν παρὰ κῦμα
ἔκλαυσεν μήτηρ μυρία Λυσιδίκη,
ψεύστην αὐγάζουσα κενὸν τάφον ἀλλά με δαίμων
ἄπνουν αἰθυίαις θῆκεν ὁμορρόθιον
Πνυταγόρην· ἔσχον δὲ κατʼ Αἰγαίην ἅλα πότμον,
πρυμνούχους στέλλων ἐκ Βορέαο κάλους.
ἀλλʼ οὐδʼ ὣς ναύτην ἔλιπον δρόμον, ἀλλʼ ἀπὸ νηὸς
ἄλλην πὰρ φθιμένοις εἰσανέβην ἄκατον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.384: ἡ Βρόμιον στέρξασα πολὺ πλέον
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
ἡ Βρόμιον στέρξασα πολὺ πλέον ἢ τροφὸς Ἰνώ,
ἡ λάλος ἀμπελίνη γρῆυς Ἀριστομάχη,
ἡνίκα τὴν ἱερὴν ὑπέδυ χθόνα, πᾶν τʼ ἐμαράνθη
πνεῦμα πάρος κυλίκων πλεῖστον ἐπαυρομένῃ,
εἶπε τάδʼ· “ὦ Μινοῖ, πῆλαι, φέρε, κάλπιν ἐλαφρὴν
οἴσω κυάνεον τοὐξ Ἀχέροντος ὕδωρ·
καὐτὴ παρθένιον γὰρ ἀπώλεσα.” τοῦτο δʼ ἔλεξε
ψευδές, ἵνʼ αὐγάζῃ κἠν φθιμένοισι πίθον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.395: οὗτος ὁ Καλλαίσχρου κενεὸς τάφος,
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
οὗτος ὁ Καλλαίσχρου κενεὸς τάφος, ὃν βαθὺ χεῦμα
ἔσφηλεν Λιβυκῶν ἐνδρομέοντα πόρων,
συρμὸς ὅτʼ Ὠρίωνος ἀνεστρώφησε θαλάσσης
βένθος ὑπὸ στυγερῆς οἴδματα πανδυσίης.
καὶ τὸν μὲν δαίσαντο κυκώμενον εἰν ἁλὶ θῆρες,
κωφὸν δὲ στήλη γράμμα λέλογχε τόδε.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.403: Ψύλλος, ὁ τὰς ποθινὰς ἐπιμισθίδας
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
Ψύλλος, ὁ τὰς ποθινὰς ἐπιμισθίδας αἰὲν ἑταίρας
πέμπων ἐς τὰ νέων ἡδέα συμπόσια,
οὗτος ὁ θηρεύων ἀταλόφρονας, ἐνθάδε κεῖται,
αἰσχρὸν ἀπʼ ἀνθρώπων μισθὸν ἐνεγκάμενος.
ἀλλὰ λίθους ἐπὶ τύμβον, ὁδοιπόρε, μήτε σὺ βάλλε,
μήτʼ ἄλλον πείσῃς· σῆμα λέλογχε νέκυς.
φεῖσαι δʼ οὐχ ὅτι κέρδος ἐπῄνεσεν, ἀλλʼ ὅτι κοινὰς
θρέψας, μοιχεύειν οὐκ ἐδίδαξε νέους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.87: μηκέτι νῦν μινύριζε παρὰ δρυΐ,
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
μηκέτι νῦν μινύριζε παρὰ δρυΐ, μηκέτι φώνει
κλωνὸς ἐπʼ ἀκροτάτου, κόσσυφε, κεκλιμένος·
ἐχθρόν σοι τόδε δένδρον ἐπείγεο δʼ, ἄμπελος ἔνθα
ἀντέλλει γλαυκῶν σύσκιος ἐκ πετάλων
κείνης ταρσὸν ἔρεισον ἐπὶ κλάδον;, ἀμφὶ τʼ ἐκείνῃ
μέλπε, λιγὺν προχέων ἐκ στομάτων κέλαδον.
δρῦς γὰρ ἐπʼ ὀρνίθεσσι φέρει τὸν ἀνάρσιον ἰξόν,
ἁ δὲ βότρυν στέργει δʼ ὑμνοπόλους Βρόμιος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.161: Ἡσιόδου ποτὲ βίβλον ἐμαῖς ὑπὸ
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
Ἡσιόδου ποτὲ βίβλον ἐμαῖς ὑπὸ χερσὶν ἑλίσσων
Πύρρην ἐξαπίνης εἶδον ἐπερχομένην
βίβλον δὲ ῥίψας ἐπὶ γῆν χερί, τοῦτʼ ἐβόησα·
ἔργα τί μοι παρέχεις, ὦ γέρον Ἡσίοδε;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.221: Αὐγάζω τὸν ἄφυκτον ἐπὶ σφραγῖδος
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
Αὐγάζω τὸν ἄφυκτον ἐπὶ σφραγῖδος Ἔρωτα
χερσὶ λεοντείαν ἁνιοχεῦντα βίαν,
ὡς τᾷ μὲν μάστιγα κατʼ αὐχένος, ᾇ δὲ χαλινοὺς
εὐθύνει· πολλὰ δʼ ἀμφιτέθηλε χάρις.
φρίσσω τὸν βροτολοιγὸν ὁ γὰρ καὶ θῆρα δαμάζων
ἄγριον, οὐδʼ ὀλίγον φείσεται ἁμερίων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.229: ἀρχαίη σύνδειπνε, καπηλικὰ μέτρα φιλεῦσα,
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
ἀρχαίη σύνδειπνε, καπηλικὰ μέτρα φιλεῦσα,
εὔλαλε, πρηΰγελως, εὔστομε, μακροφάρυξ,
αἰὲν ἐμῆς πενίης βραχυσύμβολε μύστι, λάγυνε,
ἦλθες ὅμως ὑπʼ ἐμὴν χεῖρά ποτε χρόνιος.
αἴθʼ ὄφελες καὶ ἄμικτος ἀνύμφευτός τε παρείης,
ἄφθορος ὡς κούρη πρὸς πόσιν ἐρχομένη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.246: Ἐθραύσθης, ἡδεῖα παρʼ οἰνοπόταισι λάγυνε,
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
Ἐθραύσθης, ἡδεῖα παρʼ οἰνοπόταισι λάγυνε,
νηδύος ἐκ πάσης χευαμένη Βρόμιον.
τηλόθε γὰρ λίθος εἰς σὲ βαρύστονος, οἷα κεραυνός,
οὐ Διὸς ἐκ χειρῶν, ἀλλὰ Δίωνος ἔβη.
ἦν δὲ γέλως ἐπὶ σοὶ καὶ σκώμματα πυκνά, τυπείσης,
καὶ πολὺς ἐξ ἑτάρων γινόμενος θόρυβος.
οὐ θρηνῶ σε, λάγυνε, τὸν εὐαστῆρα τεκοῦσαν
Βάκχον, ἐπεὶ Σεμέλη καὶ σὺ πεπόνθατʼ ἴσα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.270: κωμάζω, χρύσειον ἐς ἑσπερίων χορὸν
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
κωμάζω, χρύσειον ἐς ἑσπερίων χορὸν ἄστρων
λεύσσων, οὐδʼ ἄλλων λὰξ ἐβάρυνʼ ὀάρους·
στρέψας δʼ ἀνθόβολον κρατὸς τρίχα, τὴν κελαδεινὴν
πηκτίδα μουσοπόλοις χερσὶν ἐπηρέθισα.
καὶ τάδε δρῶν εὔκοσμον ἔχω βίον οὐδὲ γὰρ αὐτὸς
κόσμος ἄνευθε λύρης ἔπλετο καὶ στεφάνου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.286: ὄρνι, τί μοι φίλον ὕπνον
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
ὄρνι, τί μοι φίλον ὕπνον ἀφήρπασας; ἡδὺ δὲ Πύρρης
εἴδωλον κοίτης ᾤχετʼ ἀποπτάμενον.
ἢ τάδε θρέπτρα τίνεις, ὅτι θῆκά σε, δύσμορε, πάσης
ᾠοτόκου κραίνειν ἐν μεγάροις ἀγέλης;
ναὶ βωμὸν καὶ σκῆπτρα Σαράπιδος, οὐκέτι νυκτὸς
φθέγξεαι, ἀλλʼ ἕξεις βωμὸν ὃν ὠμόσαμεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.554: Λάθριος Ἡράκλεια καλῶν ὑπὸ χείλεσιν
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.732: βουκόλον ἢν ἐσίδῃς τὸν ἐμόν,
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
βουκόλον ἢν ἐσίδῃς τὸν ἐμόν, ξένε, τοῦτʼ ἔπος αὐτῷ
εἶπον, ὅθʼ ὁ πλάστης ὧδὲ μʼ ἔδησε Μύρων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca X.4: λῦσον ἀπʼ εὐόρμων δολιχὰ πρυμνήσια
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
λῦσον ἀπʼ εὐόρμων δολιχὰ πρυμνήσια νηῶν,
εὔτροχα δʼ ἐκπετάσας λαίφεα ποντοπόρει,
ἔμπορεʼ χειμῶνες γὰρ ἀπέδραμον, ἄρτι δὲ κῦμα
γλαυκὸν θηλύνει πρηΰγελως Ζέφυρος·
ἤδη καὶ φιλότεκνος ὑπὸ τραυλοῖσι χελιδὼν
χείλεσι καρφίτην πηλοδομεῖ θάλαμον
ἄνθεα δʼ ἀντέλλουσι κατὰ χθόνα· τῷ σὺ Πριήπῳ
πειθόμενος πάσης ἅπτεο ναυτιλίης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca X.18: Γῶβρυ, Διώνυσός σε καὶ ἡ
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
Γῶβρυ, Διώνυσός σε καὶ ἡ φιλεράστρια Κύπρις
τέρποι, καὶ γλυκεραὶ γράμμασι Πιερίδες·
ὧν μὲν γὰρ σοφίην ἀποδρέπτεο· τῆς δʼ ἐς ἔρωτας
ἔρχεο· τοῦ δὲ φίλας λαβροπότει κύλικας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.26: σφάλλομαι ἀκρήτῳ μεμεθυσμένος· ἀλλὰ τίς
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
σφάλλομαι ἀκρήτῳ μεμεθυσμένος· ἀλλὰ τίς ἆρα
σώσει μʼ ἐκ Βρομίου γυῖα σαλευόμενον;
ὡς ἄδικον θεὸν εὗρον, ὁθείνεκεν αὐτὸς ἐγὼ σέ,
Βάκχε, φέρων ὑπὸ σοῦ τἄμπαλι παρφέρομαι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.28: πέντε θανὼν κείσῃ κατέχων πόδας,
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
πέντε θανὼν κείσῃ κατέχων πόδας, οὐδὲ τὰ τερπνὰ
ζωῆς, οὐδʼ αὐγὰς ὄψεαι ἠελίου·
ὥστε λαβὼν Βάκχου ζωρὸν δέπας ἕλκε γεγηθώς,
Κίγκιε, καλλίστην ἀγκὰς ἔχων ἄλοχον.
εἰ δέ σοι ἀθανάτου σοφίης νόος, ἴσθι Κλεάνθης
καὶ Ζήνων ἀίδην τὸν βαθὺν ὡς ἔμολον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.320: Ἀντιγόνην ἔστεργε Φιλόστρατος· ἦν δʼ
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
Ἀντιγόνην ἔστεργε Φιλόστρατος· ἦν δʼ παλαισταῖς
ὁ τλήμων Ἴρου πέντε πενιχρότερος.
εὗρε δʼ ὑπὸ κρυμοῦ γλυκὺ φάρμακον ἀντία γὰρ σχὼν
γούνατʼ ἐκοιμήθη, ξεῖνε, μετʼ Ἀντιγόνης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.105: ἄλλος ὁ Μηνοφίλας λέγεται παρὰ
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
ἄλλος ὁ Μηνοφίλας λέγεται παρὰ μαχλάσι κόσμος,
ἄλλος, ἐπεὶ πάσης γεύεται ἀκρασίης.
ἀλλʼ ἴτε Χαλδαῖοι κείνης πέλας· ἦ γὰρ ὁ ταύτης
οὐρανὸς ἐντὸς ἔχει καὶ κύνα καὶ διδύμους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.241: Ὥριμος. Οἶδα καὶ αὐτός, ὁδοιπόρε.
poems.author: Marcus Argentarius
poems.text:
Ὥριμος. Οἶδα καὶ αὐτός, ὁδοιπόρε. μηκέτʼ ἐπαίνει
ἰσχάδα, μηδʼ ἐσόρα τὸν πέλας ἀκρέμονα·
καὶ λίην ὁ Πρίηπος ἐφίσταμαι ὀξὺ δεδορκὼς,
καὶ φυλακὴν σύκων ἣν ἐπέοικεν ἔχων.
ἢν δὲ μόνον σὺ θίγῃς τῆς ἰσχάδος, ἰσχάδα δώσεις·
ὡς ἰσότης πάντων ἐστὶ δικαιοτάτη.
